# Binding and Ornamentation

The exterior of this manuscript is bound in a dark brown **<term>leather binding<note>The outer protective and decorative covering of the book, here featuring a "pebbled grain" texture.</note></term>** that has been richly decorated with intricate **<term>gold-tooling<note>Also known as "gilt," this is a technique where gold leaf is pressed into the leather using heated brass stamps or wheels.</note></term>**.

A thin, double-line **<term>fillet<note>A plain decorative line or border impressed into the book cover.</note></term>** border frames the entire cover. At each of the four corners, the binder has stamped delicate floral sprigs, featuring five-petaled blossoms and small, elegant leaves.

->**The Central Motif**<-

In the center of the cover is a prominent, symmetrical **<term>lozenge-shaped<note>A diamond or rhomboid decorative element.</note></term>** ornament. This centerpiece consists of elaborate **<term>foliate scrolls<note>Decorative patterns consisting of leaf and vine-like shapes.</note></term>** and winding **volutes** that radiate from a central starburst or floral boss. Small gold dots and circular accents are interspersed within the scrollwork to catch the light.

<note>Condition Note: The left edge of the binding, where the spine meets the hinge, shows significant wear and cracking. In some areas, the leather surface has been lost, revealing the underlying material of the binding structure.</note>

# The Bookplate of Thomas South

The interior of the front cover is lined with vibrant marbled endpaper, featuring swirling patterns of blue, red, yellow, and white. This decorative paper was a common feature in high-quality bookbinding, created by floating pigments on water before transferring them to the page.

Pasted onto this marbled surface is a printed bookplate, serving as a mark of ownership and a statement of the owner's interests.

->This is the labor, this is the task<-
<note>original: "HIC LABOR HOC OPUS EST" — This is a famous quotation from the Roman poet Virgil’s *Aeneid*. In its original context, it refers to the great difficulty of returning from the underworld; here, it likely signifies the arduous effort required for spiritual or intellectual study.</note>

The bookplate features an heraldic crest at the top, showing a dragon’s head with a protruding tongue emerging from a **<term>foliated coronet<note>A small crown decorated with leaf-like shapes, used in heraldry to denote a specific rank or status.</note></term>**.

Below the crest sits the central motif: an **<term>Ouroboros<note>An ancient symbol depicting a serpent eating its own tail. It traditionally represents eternity, the cyclical nature of the universe, and the "Great Work" in alchemy.</note></term>**. This serpent forms a perfect circle, enclosing a radiant eight-pointed star that emits beams of light.

->**Thomas South.**<-
<note>Thomas South (1785–1855) was a known scholar of alchemy and the father of Mary Anne Atwood, a prominent writer on hermetic philosophy.</note>

<summary>This page describes the interior front cover and the personal bookplate of Thomas South, which features alchemical symbolism and a Latin motto from Virgil.</summary>

## FRIEDRICH ROTH-SCHOLTZ
->Engraved by I. F. Schmidt<- <note>The abbreviation "sc." in the original "I. F. Schmidt sc." stands for the Latin *sculpsit*, meaning "he engraved this." Johann Friedrich Schmidt (1706–1775) was a specialist in portrait engravings.</note>

*This engraving depicts Friedrich Roth-Scholtz (1687–1736), a significant figure in the history of science and printing. Based in Nuremberg, he was a prolific bookseller and editor who dedicated much of his life to collecting and preserving hermetic and alchemical manuscripts that might otherwise have been lost to time. He is shown here in his natural element: a scholar's study packed with bound volumes, emphasizing his status as a man of letters.*

<note>The mottos pinned to the shelves reflect the Enlightenment-era belief in the power of study. The first suggests that the contents of his books are intended for those with the wisdom to understand them, while the second identifies reading as the essential "nourishment" for practical success and intellectual growth.</note>

# Preface

->)( 3<-

Just as we now [receive] from eternal Wisdom and heavenly happiness through the true Word of **GOD**—which has been left to us through Moses, the prophets, evangelists, apostles, and through the self-subsisting Word of eternal Truth itself, our Savior and Redeemer **Christ JESUS**, for our instruction, as a rule and a guiding line;

So too has the wisdom for temporal happiness (b) been clearly described and recorded for us in the writings of the true philosophers and **students of nature** <term>Natur-Kündigern</term> <note>original: *Natur-Kündigern*; literally "nature-knowers," referring to those who study the secrets of the physical world and alchemy</note>. Within these works, seekers who love the truth have found it, still find it, and also possess it; even though many thousands will cry out to me that they have not yet found such things. But it happens here just as it does with the prophetic and other books of Holy Scripture, which are nonetheless all in German, just as—

# Friederich Roth-Scholtz’s

in the written, wandering <note>original: *Vagantischen*; refers to itinerant charlatans or "sooty-alchemists" who traveled from town to town selling fraudulent secrets.</note> false **recipes** and **processes**, (d) this you may surely believe; whoever now wishes to know the reason, ground, and foundation of this matter, let him not be weary of reading (e) them.

(d) Regarding **recipes** and **processes**, nothing of the sort shall appear in our **German THEATRUM CHEMICUM** <note>original: *THEATRO CHEMICO*; Roth-Scholtz’s famous multi-volume collection of alchemical texts published in the early 1700s.</note>. But Mr. Dr. **Becher** himself knew nothing of them; although he was otherwise a profoundly learned man in the **art of separation** <term>art of separation</term> <note>original: *Scheide-Kunst*; a contemporary term for chemistry, specifically the practical skill of refining and separating metals.</note> and in many other sciences, in which regard I wish to say nothing detrimental of him here. (e) The writings of the **philosophers** <note>In alchemical literature, "philosophers" refers to true masters of the art, as opposed to mere "laborants" or chemists.</note> require being read with great attention and often repeated, if one intends to draw any benefit or pleasure from them. [if you] do not wish to seek true **wisdom** and the great **mysteries of Nature** among the true **philosophers** <note>In this context, "philosophers" refers to "philosophers by fire" or true alchemists who seek understanding of the natural world, rather than just gold-making.</note>, but instead cling only to the **sophistical process-mongers**, who are deceivers, promising golden mountains to others while possessing nothing but ignorance as their greatest wealth, then they will give you the **beggar’s staff** <note>original: *Bettelstab*; a common 18th-century idiom meaning to be reduced to total bankruptcy and forced into vagrancy.</note> to carry in your hand, just as they carry it themselves. # Friedrich Roth-Scholtz’s [Preface]

...equally briefly, yet thoroughly in few words, [I] have said what I considered necessary to be here. Count BERNHARD <note>Bernhard Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist whose works were highly influential in the early modern period.</note> writes in the second part of his book: “In short, whoever understands the **philosophers** <note>original: *Philosophos*; here referring to the true masters of alchemy or "philosophy by fire."</note> correctly, sees without spectacles.”

I find one more thing necessary to remind [the reader] of: that in this **THEATRUM CHEMICUM** <note>The *Theatrum Chemicum* was Roth-Scholtz’s massive multi-volume project to preserve and clarify alchemical knowledge for future generations.</note> on page 130, it was promised in the notes that the following should also be incorporated into this first part, namely: 

I. The chemical writings of **JOHANNES TICINENSIS** <note>Johann von Teetz, a 14th-century priest and alchemist from Bohemia.</note>. 

II. **ANTONIUS DE ABBATIA’S** <note>A 14th-century Italian alchemist known for his letters on the "Great Work."</note> Epistle on the **Transmutation of Metals**. 

III. **EDWARD KELLEY’S** <note>Edward Kelley (1555–1597), the English alchemist and associate of John Dee.</note> treatise on the **Philosopher’s Stone** <note>original: *Stein der Weisen*</note>, along with the cautionary preface against the **sophists** <note>In alchemy, "sophists" were those who used false logic or trickery to claim they could make gold, as opposed to the "true philosophers."</note> and deceivers.

X. **ARTEPHIUS**, the ancient philosopher's *Secret Main Key* to the hidden <term>Philosopher's Stone</term>. Translated from the Latin and English editions of **Mr. WILLIAM SALMON**, Professor of Physics, into German by **Benjamin Roth-Scholtz**. 8vo <note>This "8" refers to octavo, a book size where the printed sheet is folded three times to create eight leaves.</note>. # Brief Outline
## of all the subject matter which is dealt with in the present Historical and Political Investigation of Alchemy.

§. 1. The reason why this treatise was written.
§. 2. The art of gold-making is prohibited in ecclesiastical law. <note>Ecclesiastical law refers to Canon Law; the church often viewed alchemy with suspicion due to its association with fraud or the demonic.</note>
§. 3. In the English laws it is rejected, and yet at times it has been commanded to be practiced. <note>This refers to the "Act Against Multipliers" (1404) which forbade the "multiplication" of gold and silver, though English monarchs often granted special licenses to alchemists they favored.</note>
§. 4. It is everywhere contested and rejected by the learned.
§. 5. It is attacked, and also defended, in entire volumes.
§. 6. The wretched condition of gold-makers brings their art into disrepute. <note>A common criticism in the 18th century was that alchemists promised wealth but often lived in poverty themselves.</note>
§. 7. More sensible men, however, do not let themselves be bothered by this.
§. 8. One cannot prove with philosophical arguments that the transmutation of metals is contrary to nature.
§. 9. Whether, because of the obscurity of alchemical writings, one can rightly consider this art suspicious.
§. 10. One comes to experience and examples: Whether even in ancient Egyptian wisdom <note>original: "Welt-Weißheit"</note> and Greek...

### § 4.

However, if we now dispense with all digressions and take up the matter itself, we must examine alchemy more closely before we offer its actual definition, and consider whether it turns out to be to the benefit or detriment of a realm, and whether those who practice this art should be tolerated in the land. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the reputation of alchemy, moving from the literature of the art to the visible, often tragic results of its pursuit. It specifically addresses why many people are repelled by the practice after witnessing the physical and financial ruin of its practitioners.</meta>

<page-num>15</page-num>

<header>An Examination of Alchemy.</header>

### §. 6.

The wretched state in which most alchemists find themselves repels many people and causes them to hold this art in no high regard. For it indeed happens to many that, once they have entrusted their splendid estates and commercial goods—along with all their paternal and maternal inheritance—to the smoke and the ash, while simultaneously flattering themselves that their great toil and labor will soon be heartily repaid with rich gold, and that their lives will not only be rejuvenated but also placed in a state of perpetual health, they must finally, after time and expenses have vanished, feel so great a change in themselves. Whereby they are cast into a powerless old age, into hunger and nakedness, and into a form made hideous by the black vapor of the coals, stinking of sulfur, and truly crippled <note>original: *gichtbrüchige* — literally "gout-broken," referring here to the tremors and physical decay, likely caused by chronic mercury poisoning.</note> by the incessant use of mercury, along with a nose most excellently enriched with snot; they are transformed and plunged into such misery that they now risk their life for a meager pittance—the very life they previously sought to bestow upon the metals <note>This refers to the alchemical goal of "vivifying" or "perfecting" base metals into "living" gold.</note>—and instead of the Philosopher’s Stone, they must wretchedly drag themselves along with an unhealthy body; instead of the Doctor’s Hat <note>The *Doctor-Hut* was a symbol of high academic and social status; here it represents the failed dream of achieving wisdom and prestige.</note>, they must clothe themselves in a beggar's cloak. ### §. 7.

Although it now seems unnecessary to reflect further on such things, I cannot help but cite a delightful and beautiful poem in which **NATALIS COMES** <note>Natale Conti (1520–1582), an Italian mythographer whose works were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note> (q) describes the deceptions and misfortunes of the alchemists:

> *With long strides, and in the end, you achieve nothing; she*
> *Deceives you with colors, she deceives you with a thousand shapes of things.*
> *Thus Proteus is said to turn himself into many forms,*
> *When he became a dread serpent, and then water or fire.* <note>In Greek mythology, Proteus was a sea god capable of changing his shape to avoid being captured. Here, alchemy is compared to his elusive nature.</note>

> *A fatal love of gold, and savage pains,*
> *Which once the deception of this insane art has seized.*

[Scholastic] rules are of such weight and truth that anyone who fears no sin and dares to call them into doubt must be considered the worst kind of idolater. ...thing is different from another / and Nature does not work in all things in the same way. # Investigation of Alchemy.

If one wants to know what such things are supposed to mean, these people—who are otherwise very helpful and most inclined to uncover the obscure—will be ready to answer as follows: **CORSUFFLE** <note>This is an obscure alchemical term, likely derived from the Arabic "al-kuhl" (kohl) or "al-usful," appearing in texts like the *Turba Philosophorum* to describe the "Head of the Art" or the essential matter of the Stone.</note> is the head of this work and not the beginning; yet when it has contained everything within itself, one can rightly call it so. Therefore, **Corsuffle** is the complete, compounded essence which must be roasted seven times; then it <term>tinctures</term> <note>original: "tingirt"; in alchemy, to "tincture" means to transform the internal nature and outward color of a base metal into gold or silver.</note> the whole body and receives the name of a penny, an air-flower, or a gold-flower, or even an iron-flower; so it is also called lead, tin, and a thousand other names by the <term>philosophers</term> <note>original: "Weltweisen"; literally "world-wise ones," a common term for alchemists who claimed to understand the hidden laws of nature.</note>. I do not begrudge the luck of whoever understands this.

However, I freely admit that I know nothing about it, and no one will blame me for it, as I have never applied myself to these secrets. # Investigation of Alchemy.

I also do not wish to mention now the writings of **BASILIUS VALENTINUS** <note>Basilius Valentinus was a legendary 15th-century alchemist, purportedly a Benedictine monk, though his works likely appeared in the early 1600s.</note> and others, which contain countless examples for our evidence. What then is to be made of this? Should it truly be right to believe that all of these authors conspired together, as it were, to mock the world with such nonsensical words and empty riddles? One or two might indeed harbor such malice; but to hold such an opinion of all of them would be sinful. Since these cautious and wise people feared that the greatest harm might befall a realm if this art were to become too common among the people, they therefore adopted the habit of hiding it in such riddles. 

Given this situation, if we are to accept such reasons, one might indeed <term>reason</term> <note>original: "raisonniren," meaning to argue or judge logically</note> more gently about them; however, they cannot be acquitted of all blame, since it would have been better to <term>communicate</term> <note>original: "communiciren"</note> their art orally to a few persons and pass these secrets on to posterity, rather than leading others by the nose with their highly <term>obscure</term> <note>original: "obscuren," meaning dark or unintelligible</note> writings and giving many cause to squander their fortunes. Thus, it is not believable that these people—who were certainly neither fools nor unskillful men—would have, for a long duration, painted such **flasks** <note>original: "Kolben," referring to the glass retorts used in chemical distillation.</note> or hidden coral or other common things beneath them. All of this, however, brings little probability to the table and will not be able to accomplish much in this matter. For, in the first place, the interpretation of such illustrations—as with all other figures and images—is still very doubtful, so that nothing certain can be built upon them. 

Furthermore, even if an interpretation of such figures were to be entirely accurate, I do not see why one should be valued more than another, unless it could be proven with clear reasons that the inventors of such an image intended to signify this and nothing else by it. Beyond this, I am willing to believe that the ancient **Egyptians** <note>original: "Ægytier"</note> were not stupid or unskilled people; nevertheless, it often happens that one is too easily captivated by an excessive love for antiquity <note>The author is critiquing the Renaissance tendency to assume that ancient civilizations possessed a "lost" perfect science or "Prisca Sapientia."</note>, and thus views many as more wise and experienced than they were in truth. <margin>(t) In the *Survey of Chemical Writers* <note>original: "Conspectu Scriptorum Chem."</note> Section XXIV, p. 18</margin>
written to **EDWARD IV**, was improved with notes by **IRENAEUS PHILALETHA** <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes, a pseudonym for a famous 17th-century alchemist, often identified as George Starkey.</note> and was printed in London in the year 1677, and also published in German at Leipzig in the year 1685. However, it appears that there, through an error, **RIPLEY** <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490)</note> was substituted for **LULLY** <note>Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315)</note>, since **RIPLEY** lived only 100 years after **EDWARD III**, and according to the testimony of **FRISIUS** <note>Likely the physician and bibliographer Gemma Frisius.</note> in his *Library*, he was known around the year 1490; whereas **EDWARD III** reigned as early as 1325 to 1376. But to return to our **LULLY**, scholars are still very much in disagreement regarding him, inasmuch as the nature of the times does not seem to align with such a narrative; for most historians maintain that this event took place under **EDWARD III**, who was only elevated to the throne after the death of **LULLY**, for which reason some take occasion to call this entire narrative into doubt. However, **OLAUS BORRICHIUS** <note>Olaus Borrichius (1626–1690) was a Danish polymath and chemist who defended the history of alchemy.</note> seeks to maintain (t) that this occurred under King **EDWARD I**. Because it is known of this king that, while his father was still alive, he performed great deeds in Syria, and after he had fully taken possession of the realm, he intended to make an expedition to the Holy Sepulcher <note>The tomb of Jesus in Jerusalem; Edward I participated in the Ninth Crusade.</note>; so that he might not lack for money, it is said that **LULLY** transformed a great quantity of base metal into gold.

**LULLY** <note>original: "LULLIUS," referring to Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and alchemist</note> himself recounts elsewhere (vv) that he brought the Work of the **Philosopher's Stone** <note>original: "Stein der Weisen"</note> to completion in Milan in the year 1333 with several of his assistants. He confirms this very fact at the conclusion of his last testament with these words: "With the help of God, we have made a testament in England in St. Katherine's Church in London—which stands opposite that part of the Castle <note>The Tower of London</note> which lies before the Chamber—under the reign of Edward, by the Grace of God; which we have also delivered with all its parts, according to the will of God, into the hands of the King for safekeeping, in the year of Christ 1332." Whatever else might be brought against this opinion, this so learned man has quite rationally anticipated. And indeed, the testimony of those historians who mention that golden coin called the **Rose-Noble** <note>A significant English gold coin first issued by Edward III, often associated in legend with alchemical gold</note>, which was first struck under King Edward III of England, agrees quite well with this opinion. ### §. 18.

Some wish no less to count **JOHANN ARNDT**—a clergyman highly praised for his blameless conduct and honorable life as well as for his learning—both among the Rosicrucians <note>A secret brotherhood of mystics and alchemists popular in the 17th century.</note> and among the possessors of the Philosopher's Stone <term>Philosopher's Stone: a legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</term>. Whether either of these is actually the case / is almost to be doubted; and indeed, I do not see at all why one should reckon him among the Rosicrucians / since he never associated himself with them / much less / as far as I am aware / publicly praised the undertakings and counsels of this society, whether it be real or merely invented. This can in no way be disadvantageous to them, especially since it is known that both were very careful not to mix **chemical principles** with **spiritual doctrines**.

### §. 21.

However, if the alchemists could bring forth no more significant arguments to defend their art than these chemical coins, they would truly reap very little honor. For regarding those coins marked with the image of Gustavus Adolphus <note>Gustavus Adolphus (1594–1632) was the King of Sweden and a central figure in the Thirty Years' War.</note>—namely, that they were supposedly struck from chemical gold—the incomparable Georg Wolfgang Wedel <note>A famous German physician and professor at Jena, known for his skepticism toward certain alchemical claims.</note>, a man of the highest merit in medicine and other magnificent sciences, long ago presented such a knot of doubt against this claim that no one has yet been capable of untying it (i).

For firstly, he concludes from the circumstances of the times that it was impossible for Gustavus Adolphus himself to have had these coins struck, because one cannot find a single such coin that was struck before the 34th year of the seventeenth century <note>original: "sibenden Seculi" (seventh century), here referring to the 1600s/17th century</note>. On the contrary, even children are able to tell that Gustavus Adolphus had already perished in the month of November in the year 1632 at the Battle of Lützen. And yet Monconnysius <note>Balthasar de Monconys (1611–1665), a French diplomat and traveler known for his diaries.</note> says the King himself had these ducats <term>ducats: high-purity gold coins used as trade currency throughout Europe</term> struck from chemical gold. I have no hesitation in adding this as well: that the King of Sweden never even came to Lübeck; and all will agree with me...

To make this even more credible, he points to a silver groschen, **FIGURE V**, the illustration of which we have deemed worth the effort to show in the copperplate engraving.

However, he explains quite clearly what gave cause for these characters to be minted onto these coins. Specifically, around the year 1622, there were two mint-masters in Erfurt named **Ziegler** and **Weißmantel**. The latter, so that he could distinguish his own groschen from those of the other, minted the signs of sulfur 🜍 and mercury ☿ as hallmarks and tokens of the quality of his groschen. Therefore, one will see two kinds of Erfurt groschen: one without, and the other marked with the characters of sulfur 🜍 and mercury ☿, of which the latter are considered better than the former. # Investigation of Alchemy.

Regarding the medals of the Duke of Gotha, as well as those which were presented to Emperor FERDINAND III <note>Ferdinand III (1608–1657) was Holy Roman Emperor and a known patron of the sciences and alchemy; several "alchemical" coins were struck during his reign to commemorate successful transmutations.</note>, these will not cause anyone particularly much trouble, since the matter itself sufficiently proves that such things were struck to the praise and glory of chemistry; however, whether they were actually made from chemical gold <note>The author distinguishes between "natural" mined gold and "chemical" gold produced via transmutation.</note> must first be proven with truthful grounds.

### §. 22.

I would have endless work to do if I wanted to seek out all the examples and evidentiary grounds that deal with the <term>Art of Gold-making</term> <note>original: "Goldmacher-Kunst"</note>, and about which people are accustomed to speaking so much. Furthermore, I would not know to what use? For even if I were to present many hundreds of thousands of examples and experiments, the enemies of alchemy would still reject them, even if they could bring nothing further against them than merely saying: "I do not believe it." However, I maintain that, just as the freedom not to believe is by no means taken away from these people, they will also permit me to believe—at least for so long—that metals can indeed be transformed, until someone can irrefutably prove to me that such a transformation is impossible. For as far as the examples are concerned, I believe it will have been sufficiently proven that one should neither believe everything nor reject everything. If then now

# Johann Franz Buddeus

Whether such people can be found who are truly able to make gold, it remains our duty to explain whether these people can be tolerated in a common wealth. However, so that everything proceeds in an orderly fashion, it will be necessary to divide the <term>Alchemists</term> <note>Practitioners of alchemy, the medieval forerunner of chemistry, focused on the transmutation of base metals into gold.</note> into three distinct sorts. First, let us assume there are such alchemists who are indeed truly experienced in their art and can bring to fruition that which they promise. The second sort merely give themselves out to be such true artists; since they are the worst kind of fraudsters, they intend nothing more than to sweep clean the purses of the wealthy with their grand-sounding promises. Finally, the third category consists of those people who are neither properly informed in this art, nor have any desire to deceive anyone, yet possess such an insatiable longing to learn this art that they spend all their property and goods upon it, and finally plunge themselves into the greatest poverty and extreme want.

->§. 23.<-

To come now to the true masters of this art, one should certainly think that these ought to be retained and highly esteemed, rather than being driven away or punished, especially since they wish to be regarded as the most intelligent among the children of men; indeed, they pretend that **God** has granted the knowledge of such a secret to no one except the pious

God-fearing people, and those separated from all the vanity of the world, are the ones to whom this should be granted. And this is also the reason why those who know such an art keep it so very secret, and earnestly forbid the discovery of this mystery; indeed, they oblige those who begin to practice this art to silence with an oath, solely so that no godless or unworthy people might attain such an excellent treasure. Therefore, one reads in the *Rosary of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Rosario Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical series of illustrations and texts</note>: **Whoever reveals the secret of this art, let him be cursed and he shall die of a stroke.** And *Raymond Lully* <note>a 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note> says in his *Practice*: **You are forbidden under the penalty of a curse to reveal such things to anyone, for whoever reveals it is cursed by God.** For this reason, the *Philosophers* <note>a term alchemists used to refer to themselves and their predecessors</note> have concealed it thus, and will continue to conceal it in the future with the help of God. Likewise, in his *Theory*, he says: **I swear to you by my soul, that if you reveal this, you are damned: For it comes from God, and one has Him to thank for it.** And in his *Last Testament*: **Do not cast this treasure before the unworthy, lest God call you to judgment because of it.** Finally, one sees in the *Water-Stone of the Wise* <note>original: "Aquario sapientum," a 17th-century alchemical treatise by Johann Ambrosius Siebmacher</note> the following words: **If you [reveal] this to someone unworthy or godless...**

The legal scholars are also no less accustomed to being in dispute regarding the quality of chemical gold <note>alchemically produced gold</note> and whether it is permitted to be used in transactions, especially in buying and selling. # The First Chapter.
## Concerning the Origin of Alchemy and the Emerald Tablet.

Those who undertake to write about a subject are commonly intent, above all else, on finding sufficient evidence through which they may grant their material a sense of authority. Among these supporting reasons, antiquity is not the least. If we now examine alchemy according to this foundation, we shall find that it is one of the oldest arts. For Hermes—who received the name **Trismegistus** <note>Thrice-Greatest</note> because of his vast knowledge, and is said to have lived shortly after the time of **Noah** or, as others prefer, in the time of **Moses**—already composed the entire foundation of the great secret of the Philosopher's Stone in his **Emerald Tablet**. Although there are some who go even further and attribute its origin and invention to the Patriarchs before the Great Flood, because one can have no proof of this other than mere conjecture, it is reasonable to remain with the **Emerald Tablet** as the most certain foundation, to which most alchemists have at all times referred. The aforementioned tablet, however, reads in Latin <note>original: "in Lateinischen"</note> as follows:

> It is true, without falsehood, certain, and most true. That which is below is like that which is

The Sun is its father, the Moon its mother. The wind has carried it in its belly. Its nurse is the earth. The father of all the <term>Telesmi</term> <note>The "Telesmi" refers to the perfection or completion of the entire world; the "Great Work" of alchemy.</note> of the whole world is here. Its power is complete if it be turned into earth.

You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently and with great ingenuity. It ascends from the earth to the heaven, and again it descends to the earth, and receives the power of the higher and the lower things.

In this way you will have the glory of the whole world. Therefore all obscurity shall flee from you.

This is the strong fortitude of all fortitude. Because it will overcome every subtle thing and penetrate every solid thing.

From this shall come wonderful adaptations, the method of which is this.

# The Second Chapter.
## On the Propagation of Alchemy and its Authors.

From Hermes Trismegistus, this art was further propagated in Egypt, which in ancient times was the true seat of all arts and sciences. However, because the majority of these ancient writings were lost, partly through fire, partly through war and negligence, little more was heard of this art for many centuries <note>original: "Secula"</note>, until finally the Arabs—as the nearest neighbors of the Egyptians, to whom without doubt a...

# Report on Alchemy

Part of these writings arrived; in turn, something of them was taught; therefore the name Alchemy, as an Arabic word, took its origin: namely from the article *Al*, and *Chama*, *it burned*, *he examined by heat* <note>original: "exarsit, calore examinavit"</note>, burned, or explored through fire. Among these Arabs, the following were especially famous: **GEBER**, **AVICENNA**, **King CALID**, **SENIOR ZADITH**, the **son of HAMUEL**, and others more, as can be seen from their published writings.

However, since afterwards—when the art of printing was invented—many hidden manuscripts came to light, it was found that long before those Arabs, the ancient Greek philosophers also treated this subject, as can be sufficiently seen from the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "ex Turba Philosophorum"; a famous early Latin alchemical text claiming to record a meeting of Greek sages</note>. And it is not unbelievable that the Arabs received much from the work of these Greeks, and subsequently continued and improved upon it.

Now, after the Arabs or Saracens (as they were called later on) took possession of a good part of Spain, this art finally came to the Europeans as well. Among whom, one of the first and most famous was I. **ALBERTUS MAGNUS** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and influential medieval scholar</note>, who wrote *On Alchemy*; *The Concordance of Philosophers on the Philosophers' Stone*; *The Compound of Compounds*; *A Brief Compendium on Minerals*; and *The Book of Eight Chapters on the Philosophers' Stone*.

## The Third Chapter.

### Concerning all manner of objections made against Alchemy.

Although this art is in itself glorious and excellent, there have nonetheless been many at all times who have despised it to the highest degree. In order to destroy this science with a greater appearance of justification, they have primarily attacked the alchemists and treated them in the most shameful manner. They say it remains uncertain whether a **HERMES TRISMEGISTUS** <note>The "Thrice-Great Hermes," a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts are attributed</note> ever existed in the world. Just as this man possessed a fantastic head, so too did he invent such a foolish art, filled with strange whims and dreams of golden mountains. As for the poor **PARACELSUS**, of whom such a great fuss has been made until now, he was more of a monster than a rational human being. Like an idiot, he disregarded all studies, but rather sought his greatest joy in attacking others—who were more learned than he—in the most shameful manner with coarse insults. One should only read the Preface to the book *Paragranum* <note>The *Paragranum* (1530) is one of Paracelsus's main works, where he outlines the four pillars of medicine: Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue.</note> *Works, page 78*, and one will find that the crudest peasant-lout could not speak more coarsely than he.

He was a drunkard who rinsed his throat day and night, and he had his greatest heart's joy when he could drink in competition with the peasants in the tavern: a real swine throughout his entire life. He was a godless man who never prayed, and cared little for God and His Word: a blasphemer, a devil-banisher <note>A term for an exorcist or one who commands spirits.</note>, and a sorcerer who called the devil nothing but his comrade. This is testified in their writings by **OPORINUS**, his former servant, **Georg Vetter**, his traveling companion, and **Dr. Heinrich Bullinger** <note>Bullinger (1504–1575) was a prominent Swiss Reformer and successor to Zwingli.</note>.

As for his "great cures," it was nothing but vanity, exaggeration, and boasting; for those whom he cured did not have much to rejoice about, but for the most part died soon thereafter. Many who had very little wrong with them he so ruined that they soon after gave up the ghost.

The gallows and the raven-stone <note>The "Rabenstein" was a traditional stone execution platform</note>, as the well-deserved epitaphs of such deceivers, could bear witness to what kind of people these alchemists are. **Marcus Bragadinus Mamugna**, born in Crete, a Capuchin monk and famous alchemist, was beheaded in Munich as a fraud; **Johann Henricus Müllenfels** was hanged; to say nothing of others of the same kind who had to adorn the gallows in gilded clothes, as can be seen in histories both old and new.

Therefore, every person should rightly be on their guard against this art, through which one can not only fall into extreme poverty but also place oneself under suspicion among honest people, as if one were no better than such deceivers. There are, after all, enough means to earn money in an honest way; and it is better to gather gold from medicines <note>The author suggests that the legitimate practice of medicine/pharmacy is more profitable than alchemy</note> than to make medicines out of gold, or to lose one's gold entirely.

Who would interpret it poorly of **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and bishop recognized as a Universal Doctor of the Church</note>, **Basilius Valentinus** <note>A legendary 15th-century Benedictine monk and alchemist</note>, **Raymundus Lullius** <note>Ramon Llull, a Majorcan philosopher and Franciscan tertiary</note>, and other persons of religious orders, that they applied themselves to alchemy? If it were a forbidden art, and had it hindered them in their service to God, then it would be something that one could object to; but because it is neither of the two, I do not see why one should interpret it poorly of these good clergymen that they became alchemists. **Raymundus Lullius** and **Basilius Valentinus**, although they loved alchemy, were nonetheless pious people; one need only read **Lullius's** prayer, which he prayed every time before he administered a medicine—found in the **Chemical Theater, Volume 1, page 682** <note>original: "Theatr. Here lies buried Theophrastus Paracelsus, a famous Doctor of Medicine, who healed cruel wounds, leprosy, **gout** <note>original: "Podagra," a painful form of inflammatory arthritis</note>, dropsy <note>original: "Wassersucht," an old term for swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, and other incurable diseases with wonderful skill, and commanded his goods to be distributed among the poor; he died **in the year 1541, on the 24th of September.**

As for what concerns his other writings, one cannot deny that much is contained therein which cannot be defended, unless one were to completely overturn the literal meaning or wish to make something mystical out of it. However, because **PARACELSUS** lived at a time when great importance was placed on magic, and the same was not held to be so evil—even if at times people went too far in it—one can excuse him to some extent for doing what others of that same time also did. And the love of magic may well have been the reason that he gladly associated with those magicians. The other faults which are laid upon him—namely, that he was a drunkard and seldom went to church—are likewise not to be excused, if indeed what his adversaries write is true; nevertheless, regarding the drinking, **PARACELSUS** always had comrades enough.

That **PARACELSUS** understood alchemy is sufficiently known from his writings, and no alchemist has ever yet doubted—

### Description of the Distillation Apparatus

This technical engraving illustrates a complex **distillation** <note>the process of purifying a liquid by heating it to create vapor and then cooling the vapor to collect the condensed liquid</note> system, likely used for the preparation of the medicines or alchemical substances described in the preceding chapters.

The apparatus consists of the following components:

*   **A**: The **furnace** or cylindrical heating vessel, topped with a protective dome to concentrate the heat.
*   **B**: A small stopper or outlet at the top of the dome, used to regulate pressure or add materials.
*   The vapors exit the furnace through a side tube into a series of interconnected glass **receivers** <note>original: "receptaculum"; vessels designed to catch and cool the distilled steam</note>:
    *   **C, D, G**: The first large receiver, where the heaviest vapors begin to condense.
    *   **E**: A second spherical receiver, providing additional surface area for cooling.
    *   **F**: The third and final receiver in the sequence, used to ensure that even the most volatile spirits are captured and not lost to the air.

The entire apparatus is shown resting on a flat laboratory bench, with detailed hatching in the engraving to indicate the shadows cast by the glassware. This type of multi-vessel setup was essential for the "rectification" or repeated purification of chemical substances.

When my desire for knowledge <note>original: "Wissenschafft," here referring to systematic study or natural philosophy</note> recently led me, along with a good friend, to conduct several chemical experiments—which could serve as a touchstone <note>a metaphor for a standard of truth or quality</note> for many others—I happened at that same time to come across the three epistles of the so-called Hermetic *Confederates*. I immediately took them into my school <note>likely meaning his laboratory or place of study</note> for examination, but found that they did not hold up to scrutiny. Because of this, I was moved by good intentions to compose a lesson on the making of gold <term>Goldmachen: alchemy or chrysopoeia</term>, wherein the subject matter itself led me to contradict those gentlemen, the *Trumpeters* <note>original: "Buccinatoribus," a derogatory term for those who loudly boast of alchemical secrets without substance</note>, here and there. As the little work neared its end, I came across the *Letter to a Friend* <note>original: "Epistolam ad amicum"</note> published under the name of *Otto von Helwig*. In it, I found the vanity <note>original: "vanität"</note> of the *Trumpeters* quite well exposed and answered. I was therefore prompted to reform my essay and—so as not to do what had already been done <note>original: "ne actum agerem"</note> regarding the three epistles of the Hermetic *Confederates*—to strike out most of what I had written and instead present my intention <note>original: "intention"</note> to the well-meaning reader exactly as it now appears. However, I did not consider it out of place to first provide the aforementioned von Helwig's sentiments <note>original: "sententimenten"</note> in a few of his own short words, as follows.

# JUDGMENT
## OF MR. OTTO VON HELWIG
->Concerning the<-
## ALLIED HERMETIC DUO.

**I**n that lengthy discourse of theirs, no substance and no matter of any importance occurs by which I might suspect that the title of "Adepts of the Hermetic Science"—as they call it, and with which they have so often adorned themselves in many places—actually suits these two men. I recognize them as learned, well-read, and skilled in various languages, but strangers to the true foundation of Philosophy. And although I envy no man the name of "Hermeticist," I nevertheless believe they have the least right to it; nor do I believe any illumination of Hermetic Philosophy is to be expected from this quarter, especially since they are utterly ignorant of the core of the very brief Emerald Tablet <note>original: "tabulæ Smaragdinæ"; the Emerald Tablet is a foundational cryptic text of alchemy attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, etc. If these men are of upright heart and respected authority, as they are devoted to public offices, I pity their fate, by which they are swept away into such vain labors.

> **S**ecrets, I advise, do not create,
> Where the matter is clearly named,
> For that makes many of them err greatly,
> Those who confuse even what is clear,
> And seek out from the depths
> What lies open before their door.

## Necessary Instruction
->on<-
# Gold-making.
### The First Chapter.

->Whether it be true that a **Philosopher's Stone** <note>original: "Lapis Philosophorum"; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</note> or a **Tincture** <note>a liquid alchemical preparation with similar transmutative powers</note> has ever been found in the world? And whether gold or silver can be produced by any means of the Art?<-

->I.<-

For three consecutive years now, several persons have published three **Trumpet-Blasts** <note>original: "Epistolas Buccinatorias"; provocative open letters intended to summon or challenge others</note> in print, which seek to dismiss the art of making the **Philosopher's Stone** as a thankless devilry. In the first of these, they presume to pressure the **adepts** <note>original: "adeptos"; those who have mastered the secrets of alchemy</note> to the point of demanding that they should present the **mystery** <note>original: "mysterium"</note> to them clearly, without any reserve, and with all its circumstances. # The Second Chapter.

## Concerning those who have written about the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>Latin: Lapide Philosophorum; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</note>, and especially concerning the <term>Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross</term> <note>Latin: Fraternität Roseæ Crucis; a mysterious spiritual and cultural movement of the 17th century</note>.

<margin>1.</margin> There is nothing easier in the world than to write about the Philosopher's Stone. For just as the Jews are able to write shamelessly about the coming of their Messiah and about the precious banquet that shall then be given—as if describing a matter which is incomprehensible to human knowledge and therefore, being supernatural, must be grasped only by faith—so too do people write recklessly about the Philosopher's Stone, and every fool interprets the folly of another fool according to his own lack of understanding. For because the <term>universal matter</term> <note>Latin: Materia lapidis; the "first matter" required to begin the alchemical work</note> of the stone is universal, and the labor is an imitation of the generation of all those things which are born: therefore, let a man write as he will, it must somehow rhyme; and where it does not rhyme, it must be said to have been spoken <term>enigmatically</term> <note>Latin: ænigmaticè; in riddles or obscure metaphors</note>. Thus it is true that one can lie without shame and write whatever one wishes concerning the monarchy of the Jewish Messiah and the Philosopher's Stone. For this much is true: even the <term>adepts</term> <note>Latin: adepti; those who have mastered the secret of alchemy</note> themselves will not be able to find their way through it, because their operations are not all the same, and even their starting materials are different in substance. There will...

# Wilhelm Baron von Schröder

Therefore, so many absurdities have been put forward regarding the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>original: "Lapide Philosophorum"; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</note> that the heralds of this art are not unjustly annoyed by it.

2. For these reasons, it is truly difficult to distinguish a true <term>Philosopher</term> <note>In this context, a natural philosopher or alchemist</note> from <term>Sophists</term> <note>Deceptive or false teachers</note>, no matter who undertakes the task, as my following chapter will further demonstrate. For one philosopher does not necessarily know what the other knows; nor does one write like the other. For every bird sings according to how its beak has grown.

3. I also do not know what I should say or judge regarding the <term>Brothers of the Rosy Cross</term> <note>original: "Fratribus Roseæ crucis"; the Rosicrucians, a secret spiritual and cultural movement</note>. I must believe that they owe their origin solely to sensible <term>Philosophers</term> experienced in nature; but I am also of the persuasion that afterwards all sorts of gypsy-rabble used such a title and deceived honest people, and I know this more than too well. About twenty years ago in England, I knew one by the name of **John Heyde** <note>Likely referring to John Heydon (1629–1667), an English astrologer and Rosicrucian apologist</note>, who wrote an entire history of the <term>Brothers of the Rosy Cross</term> in a large volume, and called himself a <term>servant of God and Secretary of Nature</term> <note>original: "servum DEI & Secretarium naturæ"</note>; he miserably misled many noble people and afterwards died wretchedly, although his books are still carried around everywhere even now.

For it is and remains true: He who already knows something can perfect himself through the books of the philosophers; but he who knows nothing will hardly learn much from them. For the philosophical style <note>The "Hermetic" or coded style used by alchemists to hide their secrets from the uninitiated.</note> is this: They keep the *primary matter* <note>original: "primam materiam" — the base substance needed to start the Great Work.</note> secret and describe the process enigmatically <note>original: "ænigmaticè" — in riddles.</note>. And so that an experienced laboratory worker might not perhaps discover the material through the labor itself, they immediately patch in a common operation involving *strong waters* <note>original: "aquis fortibus" — usually refers to nitric acid or other corrosive mineral acids.</note>, sublimates, and spirits of wine, etc. What is spoken of philosophically, they explain through a common chemical operation. At one moment they speak of the *remote matter of the stone* <note>original: "materia remota lapidis"</note>, namely the raw state; the next, of the *proximate matter* <note>original: "materiâ proximâ"</note>, that is, the prepared state. Thus they mix the subjects together, by which they lead the seeker astray and deceive him. Therefore, believe the philosophers' headings, but trust nothing of their preparations. For where they speak openly, there is a deception behind it. But where they speak enigmatically, there you should reflect upon it. I would know of no better method to advise for reading such authors than that which Mr. Daniel Richter, currently Privy Councilor at Darmstadt, presented in his *New Treasury of Oratory* published at Nuremberg, regarding the reading of authors in general; let everyone take this recommendation to heart, even if it seems somewhat difficult at first. # Wilhelm, Baron von Schröder

In my youth, I had the *author* <note>original: "autorem"; likely referring to a specific teacher or the author of a foundational text</note> himself as my master in this matter, for which I am still grateful to him; for there is no other way to untangle oneself from the confused writings of the philosophers. The clearest *writers* <note>original: "Scriptores"</note> are **Raymond Lull** <note>A 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and logician to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note> and **Brother Basil Valentine** <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, purportedly a Benedictine monk, known for his writings on antimony</note>; but one must read all of their writings and see how the *Vitriol* <note>A sulfate mineral, often used as a starting point for acids</note> and the *Spirit of Mercury* <note>The volatile, essential essence of mercury sought by alchemists</note> are to be produced from a single material. **Valentine** has, in all his writings, named the *true, most universal material* <note>original: "veram materiam universalissimam"</note> by name in only one single place; and whoever takes it will nevertheless be deceived, because he has remained silent regarding the *signs* of the materials and the distinction in the *selection* <note>original: "electione"</note> of the same. Without this, knowing the material is of no use, even if it appears to be the same thing before human eyes.

5. When you have the *Material* and know how to make the *Spirit of Mercury*, you need nothing more. For **Bernard of Trevisan** <note>A 15th-century Italian alchemist famous for his lifelong quest for the Philosopher's Stone</note> teaches the rest clearly—indeed, almost more than clearly—provided that his material has come into your hands. For otherwise, every material requires a different *separation*, *purification*, and *operation*, which must rightly seem strange to one who is unacquainted with the art.

# The Third Chapter.
## How the ancient Sages arrived at the thought that metals could be ripened, and how they went to work so that they found the first matter <note>original: "primam materiam"; the fundamental substance from which all things are created</note>.

1. It is said that the title of discovery <note>original: "Titulus inventionis"</note> is often the better part of the discovery <note>original: "potior pars inventionis"</note>. Thus, since gold and silver are ripened by Nature under the earth through such a long cooking process, it is no small wonder how men arrived at the thought that one could, through Art, intercept Nature's path and produce gold and silver above the earth in such a short time. However, the old Philosophy <note>referring to traditional alchemy</note> had its beginning from speculation <note>original: "ex speculatione"</note>, just as the modern experimental Philosophy <note>original: "Philosophia experimentalis"; the emerging scientific method of the 17th century</note> has its origin from experiments <note>original: "experimentis"</note>. Therefore, the ancient Philosophers closely observed and examined the generation <note>the birth or formation</note> of metals in the earth, and found that all metals take their origin from mercury <note>original: "ex mercurio"</note>. But because they found in their operation <note>practical laboratory work</note> that mercury was already a coagulated <note>solidified</note> metal, they sought to investigate the Spirit of Mercury as its beginning. For that reason, they undertook to perform reductions <note>chemical processes to return a substance to its original state</note>, which, however, did not want to proceed correctly. Therefore, they ran back to Nature and asked the *Archaeus* <note>the "master workman" or vital force that governs the growth of minerals and life according to Paracelsus</note> for advice,

# RIDDLE.

I am the Wolf who devours all,
I thirst for the blood of my children,
Therefore I am called the Child-Eater,
By which name the world knows me.
I devour, I tear apart, I kill,
And yet I give life back again:
For nothing can live without me,
And whatever dies, it is I who kill it.
In me everything must be buried,
That wishes to have life again.
Everything that lives calls me Father,
And is daily fed by me.
Yet no one knows how to obtain me,
Until he has taken my coat from me.
Therefore it rarely happens,
That a man is ever able to see me.
<note>The "Wolf" is a common alchemical symbol for antimony or the universal solvent (acid) that "devours" metals to purify them. The "coat" refers to the outer, impure form of the matter.</note>

# Instruction on the Making of Gold.

The philosophers remained steadfast without wavering and have obtained from an *immature electrum* <note>original: "Electro immaturo"; likely referring to a natural alloy of gold and silver or a specific mineral ore</note>, both the *spirit of Mercury* <note>the volatile, life-giving essence of quicksilver</note> as well as the *seed of gold*, through long toil and labor, and great expense and immeasurable patience; for which they prepared all kinds of *solvents* <note>original: "menstrua"; substances used to dissolve or extract essences</note>. However, because it was not the true *Electrum*, they had to reach their *intention* <note>goal</note> through a detour; although such *Tinctures* <note>alchemical solutions capable of transmuting metals</note> were by no means to be compared to the *most universal* <note>original: "universalissimo"; the highest grade of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. The cause of this was that in these *electrums* the *metallic seed* was indeed still open, but already *specified* <note>fixed into a particular metallic form rather than remaining a primal substance</note>. Therefore, it could not *act so freely* and be brought into the *operation*.

2. Others wished to *correct* this error; they therefore took a *matrix of Vitriol* <note>the "womb" or source mineral of sulfates</note>, which could not be made to crystallize into *Vitriol* by any art; they *purified* it through certain very artistic maneuvers. They then drew out a *spirit of Mercury*, all of which proceeded without singular effort; they *fermented* this with the *soul of the Sun* <note>original: "anima Solis"; the essential sulfur or "soul" of gold</note>, and finally obtained a *Tincture*. This, however, *tinged* <note>transformed base metal into gold</note> very little, and over four years passed in the *operation*. They afterwards sought to remedy this through *trituration* <note>the process of grinding to a fine powder</note>, but to date they have not reached an end. The cause, however, of why it yielded so little, is the *specified Salt* which is in the *vitriolic liquor* and causes an impure *coagulation* <note>the thickening or solidifying of the substance</note>.

# Instruction on the Making of Gold.

I will mention no particular processes here which I can perform by means of common herbs, and which are otherwise attributed to the *Philosopher's Stone* <note>original: "Lapidi Philosophorum"; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</note>. How long have men remained under the impression that red glass could not be made except by the Elixir? Yet it is now almost common knowledge that it can be prepared even without the Elixir. This has only recently been very clearly described, with all the practical techniques, in a fine little treatise titled *The Sun Without Clothing* <note>original: "Sol sine veste"; a famous 17th-century work by Johann Christian Orschall concerning the production of ruby glass</note>, printed in Augsburg by . . . <note>The author leaves the name blank or it was omitted in the source</note>. On this occasion, I must report that just as the *Sulfur of the Sun* <note>original: "Sulphur Solis"; a term for the essential soul or coloring principle of gold</note> is to be found in many other metals and minerals just as well as in *gold itself* <note>original: "ipso auro"</note>, the author of that little treatise or others should not be surprised if someone can give the ruby or red color to glass even without using gold. Whoever wishes to attempt such a thing should make a red sulfur of Venus <note>term for copper</note> and use it; thus he will soon be able to help himself. 

Furthermore, in that same experiment regarding the precipitation of gold with Jove <note>term for tin</note>, a great error is found: people believe that the gold <note>original: "☉", the alchemical symbol for the Sun/Gold</note> has been made irreducible through this precipitation. However, the mixture with Jove is the only cause of this destruction <note>meaning the loss of the gold's metallic form</note>. When the Jupiter <note>tin</note> is turned to slag using niter <note>saltpeter</note>, you will find your gold in bodily form <note>original: "corporaliter"</note> just as it was before. I have only wanted to mention this here in passing.

# Wilhelm Freiherr von Schröder

2. As far as I am aware, I was the first person who, approximately 15 years ago, presented the King of England with a drinking glass made of such red glass <note>Gold-ruby glass, a prized alchemical achievement of the 17th century</note> which I had made myself; for at that time, red glass had not been shown by anyone else. It may be that one <term>Philosophus</term> <note>Philosopher; here referring to an alchemist</note> or another can apply his <term>Tinctur</term> <note>Tincture; a potent alchemical substance capable of transforming matter or curing disease</note> to something in a way that others are ignorant of doing. But this I know for certain: that one <term>Tincture</term> has different effects than another. As for Wagnereck's <note>Likely referring to a contemporary alchemist or physician</note>, I do not know if it has been used <note>original: "ad corpus humanum"</note> on the human body, which I attribute to his ignorance.

The <term>malleability</term> <note>The quality of being able to be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking</note> of glass I do not consider impossible, because I know that in my time in Amsterdam, a good friend made an <term>Aqua-fort</term> <note>original: "Aqua-fortis"; literally "strong water," usually nitric acid</note> which remained standing for several years and was not used. However, when he once cleared out his laboratory and wanted to move this glass vessel elsewhere among other things, he reached into the glass with his fingers and found that it could be bent and twisted. But as soon as the <term>Aqua-fortis</term> was removed, the glass gradually hardened again. This good friend could not recall how that <term>Aqua-fortis</term> had been made. Thus it appears that several fools have written about the <term>Lapide Philosophorum</term> <note>original: "Lapis Philosophorum"; the Philosopher's Stone</note> and yet have never seen it with their own eyes, much less made it, attributing to it all rare and unknown <term>operationes</term> <note>operations or chemical processes</note>, although

# Instruction on the Making of Gold.

Although it is a great matter to know the virtues that the **Elixir** <note>The Elixir, or the Philosopher's Stone, was believed to be a substance capable of turning base metals into gold and curing all diseases.</note> possesses within itself. My good friend in England, Mr. **Robert BOYLE** <note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691) was a founding figure of modern chemistry, though he remained deeply interested in alchemy throughout his life.</note>, informs me that several hundred virtues which the **Philosopher's Stone** <note>original: "Lapis Philosophorum"</note> is capable of were communicated to him; a knowledge which he held as highly as the **secret** <note>original: "arcanum"</note> of the **preparation** of the **Stone** itself. But it remains once and for all the case that one **Medicine**, or one **Stone**, works differently than another.

For example: those who make their **solvent** <note>original: "menstruum"; in alchemy, a solvent used to dissolve solids.</note> from the **Spirit of Urine** <note>original: "Spiritu urinæ"; ammonia or a related distillate used in chemical experiments.</note> encounter many strange **effects** in their work, such as **concerning perpetual light** <note>original: "de lumine perpetuo"; a reference to the alchemical quest for a lamp that would burn forever without being consumed.</note> and the like, which other, and indeed more precious, **Tinctures** cannot bring about. Therefore, the **writers on Tinctures** come and compile from books whatever they find, adding their own fantasies for good measure, and everything must be and remain true; thus they wish to persuade the world that the **Tincture** makes the old young, the black white, and is able to turn darkness itself into light.

Now, although this blessed **Elixir** must necessarily have many great and heavenly virtues—which, however, every **possessor** of the blessed Stone does not know—and even if he has perhaps heard of them, he still lacks the **method of application** <note>original: "am modo applicandi"</note>, which cannot be learned except through the faithful **instruction** of a good friend. There are some who attribute many and great virtues in medicine to the *materia cruda* <term>raw material: the base substance used in alchemy before it is refined</term> of the *Lapis Philosophicus* <term>Philosopher's Stone: the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and providing an elixir of life</term>. It has not been very long since the use of such materials was taken into consideration by certain physicians in Germany; but now they are beginning to write great things about them. In England, likewise, such material is exalted by some above all other medicines. However, no one knows what he has in his hands, and they undertake preparations with it whereby they ruin more than they improve. If they took the raw material and stuck with it, they would accomplish more—provided they understood the *Signa Diagnostica* <term>diagnostic signs: the specific physical indicators used to identify the correct quality of a substance</term> in selecting the material. For without such knowledge, it is as if they knew nothing. Indeed, not knowing a thing, or not knowing it correctly, is one and the same. ## The Ninth Chapter.
### Regarding the Use of the Elixir in the Human Body.

1. The common and customary way to use the <term>Elixir</term> <note>A preparation believed to prolong life or transform metals</note> or the <term>Tincture</term> <note>A concentrated medicinal or alchemical extract</note> for the human body <note>original: "ad corpus humanum"</note> is as follows: they extract and circulate the first-prepared Tincture with a highly concentrated spirit or essence of wine <note>original: "Spiritu vel essentia vini summe essensificata"; likely a high-proof distilled alcohol</note>. 2. Others, however, do not prepare <note>original: "præpariren"</note> the Tincture in any way other than specifically <note>original: "particulariter"</note> for this or that body. Namely, they prepare a solvent <note>original: "menstruum"; a substance used to dissolve or extract materials</note> from the blood of that person whose health is sought <note>original: "ex sanguine istius hominis, de cujus sanitate quæritur"</note>. With this solvent, they dissolve <note>original: "solviren"</note>, extract, and circulate the Tincture. Through this, such power and effect have been perceived in this Tincture that the Philosophers <note>The term used for alchemists and natural scientists</note> have had cause enough to write great things about it.

### Experiment III.
# A Proven Thief’s Particular.
->Called "part with part."<- <note>original: "Pars cum parte genandt." This refers to a "particular" (a specific alchemical recipe) where a portion of precious metal is combined with a base metal in such a way that the entire mass appears to be precious metal.</note>

<term>Take:</term> <note>original: "Rec." for Recipe, the standard opening for a chemical or medical formula.</note> Verdigris <note>A green pigment or crust formed by the action of acetic acid on copper.</note>, 2 lots <note>A "lot" is a historical unit of weight, roughly 14-17 grams.</note>. <term>Sal Ammoniac</term> <note>Ammonium chloride, used as a flux to clean metal surfaces.</note>, <term>Vitriol</term> <note>A term for sulfate minerals; here likely green or blue vitriol used to create acidic vapors.</note>, <term>Niter</term> <note>Saltpeter, used as a powerful oxidizing agent.</note>, 1 lot of each. # A Sincere
## Warning and Exhortation

From a faithful lover of the truth / to all true lovers of the nature of <term>Transmutational Alchemy</term> <note>original: "ALCHEMIÆ TRANSMVTATORIÆ"; the art of changing base metals into gold or silver</note>, concerning the necessity of close supervision due to the knavish maneuvers of deceitful <term>Arg-Chemists</term> <note>A play on words combining "Arge" (wicked/bad) and "Alchemist," referring to fraudulent practitioners</note>.

Dear friend / follow my sincere and highly useful teaching / if a "Gold-Beetle" <note>A derogatory term for a traveling charlatan who claims to be able to make gold</note> comes flying to you / (a) who says / he knows and wishes to teach you how to make silver and gold / do not believe everyone so quickly and easily; for it is not such a lowly art / as many allow themselves to dream. If he then offers his art of silver- and gold-making / to perform a demonstration for you / so that you shall see the truth for yourself / well then / let it be so / you can allow him to show you / however, at the artist's own expense / (b) only do not trust him any more or further / than what you see: Give him and his assistants only diligent attention regarding their fists <note>Meaning their hand movements or "sleight of hand"</note> / furnaces / instruments / tools / materials and <term>species</term> <note>The specific chemical ingredients or substances used in a reaction</note>, despite his excellent boasting.

---

<margin>(a) These Gold-Beetles do not only fly in May / but all year round.</margin>
<margin>(b) Trust is well and good / but the horse rode away <note>A proverbial warning that misplaced trust leads to loss</note>.</margin>

# Warning and Admonition

...of the examples of excessive drinking, incest <note>original: "Blut-Schande"</note>, adultery, sorcery, murder, and other coarse sins and vices, to be recorded and recounted in the Bible. God forbid that one should even think such a thing in their heart, let alone speak it. By that logic, the ancient Spartans—because they presented drunkards to their youth to inspire disgust—must have been drunkards themselves; and that certain Prince, because he displayed a "codpiece" <note>original: "Hosenputz," referring to ostentatious and indecent fashion</note> (to lead people away from shameful clothing), must have been a scoundrel himself. Not at all! On the contrary, my slanderers <note>original: "Calumnianten"</note>—to whom I have recounted such "fine little tricks" (which we and other good people have experienced passively, not actively) for the sake of my calling and office (m) as a reminder and heartfelt warning—would do well to look out for themselves: either to desist from such things, or at least not to become such fellows themselves and fall into the "Guild of Rogues." For there are those who carry out the acts I have recounted, or who engage in other similar, no better tricks in different matters; especially since some of them, perhaps out of habit, seem quite inclined and disposed toward such behavior.

The "veneration" which the wicked and "All-Ghemistical" <note>A pun on "Alchemist" and "All-Ghemist" (meaning "all-filth" or "all-rubbish")</note>, intentionally fraudulent "Guild of Gold-Beetles" <note>A derogatory term for fraudulent alchemists seeking only gold</note> feels toward me because of the publication of their—to them—highly useful...

For there is one kind of knowledge that comes from understanding, and another that comes from approval. <note>original Latin: "Non scientia mali, sed usus mali damnat. Est enim scientia alia Cognitionis, alia Approbationis."</note></margin>

# Concerning the Generation of Metals

The aforementioned sulfur acts upon the *mercury* <note>original: "Mercurium"; in alchemy, mercury represents the principle of fluidity and volatility</note>, and makes from it a stone, a block, or a lump. This is exactly as the seed of the man acts within the matter of the woman, and it *coagulates* <note>thickens or solidifies</note> into a lump or a piece of flesh, from which in time a human being is born, etc. It is the same with *mercury*: when it has become a lump through the sulfur, the heat and dryness of the sulfur overcome the cold and moisture of the *mercury*. This gives birth to the first *grade* <note>stage of development</note> of the metals, which is lead (♄). 

If the heat and dryness of the sulfur overcome yet another *grade* of the cold and moisture of the *mercury*, it creates tin (♃). Thirdly, it creates silver (☽). And from the silver (☽), gold is ultimately produced; for there is no gold that was not silver beforehand. 

As for the other two metals, they are like burnt and over-cooked metals: namely copper (♀) and iron (♂). Iron in particular is harder to bring to a flow <note>to melt</note> than copper because of its earthy, coarse, and fixed sulfur, which does not easily allow the impure mercury within it to melt. Therefore, these two metals are over-cooked; lead and tin are too little digested <note>refined by heat</note> and cooked; but silver and gold maintain the perfect middle ground between them.

For what reasons, then, has the sun (☉) <note>the alchemical symbol for gold</note> reached its *perfection* and become gold, and—

->Response<-

For this reason: gold is ripe and has reached its term, just like an apple or a pear on the tree. If one picks a pear or apple before its time, it is gritty and sour and cannot be eaten; but if one lets it hang for its duration, it becomes good and savory to eat, etc.

Gold has become the <term>ultimate matter<note>original: "ultima materia"; the final, perfected state of a substance in alchemy</note></term>, which no element can further affect or diminish; for it is fixed, and endures in the fire and all tests, as is proper for gold until the end of the world, etc.

How must I understand this?

In this way! It has passed through the seven spheres or planets of the metals; and Nature has cooked it for so long until she has again separated away the <term>sulfur<note>symbol: 🜍; representing the active, combustible principle</note></term> which brought the <term>mercury<note>symbol: ☿; representing the fluid, metallic principle</note></term> to <term>solidification<note>original: "coagulation"</note></term>, and has ignited its internal sulfur and brought it into movement, which the mercury—from which it was born—first received. And precisely in the final separation of the external, clinging, evil, and burning sulfur, the metal becomes good gold through its internal sulfur.

This is truly the generation of the metals.

## Now follows the Transmutation of Metals.

For what reasons do men wish to make or change the imperfect metals into silver and gold, and reach into God’s creation? This is not possible; if God had wanted it so, would He not have let such metals become <term>silver<note>original: ☽; the lunar symbol for silver</note></term> and <term>gold<note>original: ☉; the solar symbol for gold</note></term> within the earth?

So speak the fools and the unwise, who do not know what God has planted and hidden within Nature.

For this reason, one can transform the imperfect metals into <term>silver</term> and <term>gold</term>: because they have all grown from one root and matter—namely, from <term>Salt</term>, <term>Sulfur</term>, and <term>Mercury</term>—just as gold has. Since they all have one father and mother, just as we humans are born of father and mother, and among us are found both healthy and sick people; as all the philosophers—

# Leonhard Müllner’s Report

The philosophers compare metals to human beings, since both can be helped by the same kind of medicine, etc.

Now, if a sick person is to be restored to health, this must be done by an experienced physician <term>Medico: a doctor or healer</term> and through the means of medicine, so that the sick person may become equal to the healthy. It is exactly the same for the sick metals; they must likewise be helped through medicine or physic, just as humans are, to reach their health and perfection, so that they may become Silver <note>original symbol: ☽ (Moon)</note> and Gold <note>original symbol: ☉ (Sun)</note>.

This is natural, for there is no art on earth that follows nature more closely than this: transforming metals into silver and gold through their medicine.

# Leonhard Müllner’s Report

For this reason! Before the foundations of the world were laid, there was nothing but water, and the Spirit of God hovered upon it; then God separated the elements and made one part of the water into earth; the other part He retained to moisten the earth, so that the earth might bring forth its fruit.

In this same way our Stone is made; for we turn nature around again, and out of earth we make water again, and out of water, earth again. This is called dissolving and coagulating again. It is to be understood thus: make bodily things un-bodily—that is <term>Solution</term> <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state</note>—and conversely, make un-bodily things bodily again—that is to coagulate again. This is the whole of the Art.

For what reason do the Philosophers compare this Art to the creation of man?

For this reason: because God the Almighty took an extract of the earth and made man into an image like Himself from it! In the same way, we also take an extract of the earth and make the wise Stone from it. How else would it drive away all the sicknesses of men and transform the imperfect metals into silver and gold, if it were not of his nature? etc.

For what reasons do the Philosophers compare the <term>Stone to Christ</term> <note>original: "Lapidem Christum". A common alchemical allegory where the Stone's perfection and healing power mirror the purity and redemptive nature of Christ.</note>?

For this reason: because Christ was born of a pure virgin without any sin, without any man’s seed.

# On the Generation of Metals

Thus our Stone <note>original: "Lapis"; the Philosopher's Stone</note> is conceived from a pure matter and brings itself forth, without the addition of any other thing!

**What does the little word "Stone" signify?**

This: because everything is within it that belongs to its perfection, and it is composed of the four elements, etc.

**Why is it called a Viscous Humidity?**

Because other humidities easily smoke away and vanish from the fire, but this one does not; rather, it is made fixed and constant therein, etc.

**Why do the Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval alchemists</note> call it a medium between the metal and Mercury?**

Because Mercury cannot become any metal without Sulfur.

**Why do the Philosophers not also take Mercury and Sulfur for their Stone when they wish to make it?**

Because they do not wish to *make* metals, but rather to *transform* the metals into silver and gold; for the metals are previously nothing else than a coagulated Mercury <note>The theory that all metals are composed of varying purity levels of Mercury and Sulfur</note>; thus these two, namely Mercury and Sulfur, are already enclosed by nature in the one matter; mark this secret well.
